## Start with a specific question

**LeetCode 528 — Random Pick with Weight.** We will reason from a very small example rather than introduce a complicated notation first.

## What the obvious approach overlooks

Choosing a uniformly random index ignores different requested weights; a bucket-by-bucket simulation is wasteful for many queries.

## One simple idea

Build cumulative weights so each integer ticket from 1 to total weight corresponds to exactly one index, then use binary search to find its owner.

Before reading symbols, explain the intended operation aloud. If you can say which information is saved and which work is avoided, you have the core intuition.

## Formula and immediate translation

$$
P(I=i)=\frac{w_i}{\sum_jw_j}
$$

**Symbols and notation:** I is the sampled index; w_i is its nonnegative weight; the denominator is total positive weight over all indices; P is a probability.

**Insert actual numbers:** For weights [1,3,2], total weight=1+3+2=6. Index 0 has probability 1/6, index 1 probability 3/6=1/2, index 2 probability 2/6=1/3. Ticket ranges are [1],[2,3,4],[5,6].

This numerical calculation is essential: the expression must mean the same thing when evaluated by hand and when written in code.

## Why the mathematics leads to an algorithm

Each ticket maps to one index and index i receives exactly w_i tickets; a uniform ticket therefore implements the requested distribution.

This argument is the bridge between 'the equation looks plausible' and 'the result is correct for all inputs satisfying the assumptions'.

console.log(lowerBound([1,4,6],5));

Run from a saved `.mjs` file inside this topic directory. The exported operation is tested with Node's standard test runner. Some examples illustrate a prerequisite rather than the entire specialised algorithm; in that case, the mathematical model above remains the definition of the full task.

## Complexity and correctness boundaries

**Work bound:** O(n) preprocess cumulative sums, O(log n) per weighted sample using binary search, O(n) memory.

**Counterexample or limitation:** A sample showing approximate frequencies after 10 draws does not PROVE correctness. Beware floating-point edge cases and ensure total weight>0.

Always declare the input domain first. For example, a modulus must be positive, a probability denominator nonzero and a character indexing convention fixed. Many seemingly clever solutions fail because these conditions were never stated.
